title: The structures of ecteinascidin anticancer agents bound to DNA shed light on their mechanism of action.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded 9T8F.cif from the Protein Data Bank (PDB, the public archive of experimental 3D structures): 388,201 bytes, 3,002 atom lines, 8 DNA chains (4 duplexes), X-ray at 2.40 Angstrom. Queried the PDB metadata interface for all three entries: 9T8F (trabectedin, 2.4 A, 1,893 deposited atoms), 9T8E (lurbinectedin, 2.3 A, 518 atoms), 9T9D (PM54, 2.1 A, 1,172 atoms), all released 2026-07-29. Searched the full open-access text for every quantitative table and for the melting-temperature data.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The Foerster resonance energy transfer (FRET) melting results and the gel-shift binding results: the text says 'several DNA scaffolds containing one to three guanine bases' were tested and that three sequence designs were re-tested in four methylation states, but the actual change-in-melting-temperature numbers appear only in Figure 2 bar panels. Supplementary Table S1 (the sequence list) and S2 (crystallographic statistics) were never retrieved: the Europe PMC supplementary-files endpoint timed out twice, so I recorded the supplement as not retrievable rather than retry further.

a1_downloadable.note: Pass, verified: all three coordinate files are freely downloadable from the PDB with no login; I opened 9T8F.cif myself.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Fail. The quantity a model would predict (change in DNA melting temperature, or binding strength) is not a column in any downloadable file. It exists as bar heights in Figure 2 panels and would have to be digitised from the figure or re-derived from raw plate reads that were not deposited.

a3_inputs_present.note: Pass in principle: DNA sequences are short and written in the text or the supplementary sequence list, and the three drug structures are in the coordinate files as chemical components.

a4_units_stated.note: Pass from the text: melting-temperature shift is in degrees Celsius and gel-shift affinity is described as micromolar; crystallographic resolution is in Angstrom in the files.

a5_enough_rows.note: Fail, decisively. Three crystal structures. The largest possible labelled set is the melting assay: a handful of sequence scaffolds times three compounds, plus three designs times four methylation states times three compounds, which is on the order of 50-100 measurements at the very most, versus the 400-row floor for classification and 1,500 for regression.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Pass trivially: the three structure files total roughly 1 MB. Size was never the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be checked for the assay data because the assay numbers were never deposited and the supplement did not retrieve; the paper never states how many sequences were tested, only 'several'. The three structures do match the paper.

a8_label_provenance.note: Pass on provenance: the melting shift is a direct physical fluorescence measurement and the structures are experimental X-ray data, not another model's output. Provenance is the one thing that is clean.

existing_models.name: DeepPBS (geometric deep learning of protein-DNA binding specificity, Nature Methods 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not assessed in detail; retrieved only as a search result. It predicts sequence preference from protein-DNA structures, so it is adjacent rather than the same task (small molecule, not protein).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read in full; not quoted here.

existing_models.name: Molecular modelling and quantitative structure-activity (QSAR) approaches for DNA minor-groove binders (review, Curr Med Chem 2007; evaluation study, PubMed 20145816)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved beyond title and abstract listing. These are docking/force-field and regression approaches to minor-groove binder sequence selectivity, i.e. the closest prior art to the task considered here.

backbone.name: None proposed; a DNA language model (for example DNABERT-2) plus a molecular encoder (for example ChemBERTa) would be the obvious pair, but with three compounds and tens of sequences there is nothing to fit a head on.
backbone.hardware: CPU would be ample, which is irrelevant given the sample size.

integration.partner_dataset: PDB (DNA-ligand complexes) and PubChem/ChEMBL for the three compounds
integration.join_key: PDB chemical component identifier and InChIKey
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: A credible bigger question exists, namely whether covalent minor-groove binder sequence preference can be predicted across compound generations, but these three structures contribute three data points to it rather than a dataset.

controls.positive_control: Would have been the textbook preference for a guanine in a 5'-NGC/NGG context, which the paper itself confirms, so the model would have little left to discover.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is meaningless at this sample size; with roughly 50 measurements the shuffled and real models are statistically indistinguishable.
controls.external_validation: Older trabectedin-DNA nuclear magnetic resonance and modelling studies exist in the literature, but they report different measurement types and were not assembled into a joinable set.

honest_claim_h3: No honest model claim is available: with three crystal structures and a few dozen melting-temperature measurements that exist only as figure bars, anything fitted here would describe the figure rather than the chemistry.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a DNA sequence and a drug's chemical structure to predict how strongly the drug sticks to and stabilises that DNA.
plain_idea.train_on: What I considered: each example would be one short double-stranded DNA sequence paired with one ecteinascidin drug (a marine-derived anticancer alkaloid). Verified count of examples: 3 crystal structures; the melting-assay examples are roughly 50-100 by my reading of the text, and the exact number is unknown because the supplement did not retrieve.
plain_idea.predict: The rise in the temperature at which the DNA double helix comes apart when the drug is bound, measured by a fluorescence melting assay in which one DNA strand carries a light-emitting dye and the other a quencher.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Medicinal chemists designing next-generation ecteinascidins would want to know which DNA sequences a new analogue will prefer before synthesising it; the paper's structures do inform that, but as mechanism, not as training data.

more_or_better_data.why: Three structures and tens of melting measurements is far less data than the docking and quantitative structure-activity work already published on minor-groove binders, and less than the thousands of DNA-ligand entries already in the PDB.

confidence_score.why: No replicate-level numbers were deposited, so per-prediction uncertainty cannot be estimated from these files at all.

models_beatable.why: The prior art is largely 2007-2010 force-field and regression work, which would be beatable in principle, but not with a dataset of this size; DeepPBS (2024) is modern and open but solves the protein-DNA version of the problem.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on every condition: no existing model runs as a baseline on this exact task, the new measurements are not in machine-readable form, and there is no shared evaluation split.

ml_idea: The idea considered and rejected: predict covalent minor-groove binder sequence selectivity (melting-temperature shift, or preferred guanine context) from DNA sequence plus compound structure, using the three new drug-DNA crystal structures as structural priors. It dies on sample size. The structures themselves are genuinely valuable as three extra entries in a future PDB-wide DNA-ligand modelling effort, and that is the right way to use them: as a few rows contributed to someone else's large dataset, not as a project of their own.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed beyond the one coordinate-file download: the whole dataset is about 1 MB of text, so compute is free. The eight hours is the cost of digitising melting-temperature values out of Figure 2 bar panels, which is exactly the work that makes the label untrustworthy.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the labelled measurements, which takes five minutes: three deposited structures, and a melting assay whose numbers were never deposited in any table. That count kills it before any download.

verdict_reason: Part A fails on A5 (sample size), A2 (the label is not a column) and A7 (assay counts unverifiable). This is a three-structure crystallography paper: the coordinates download cleanly and the science is sound, but the quantity a model would predict exists only as bar heights in a figure, and even if digitised perfectly it would amount to perhaps 50-100 measurements across 3 compounds. No split, control or honest claim survives at that size.
